terminal.description: A shell in your workspace. Build the intake here, run it and type the answers. Ctrl+C stops a program that waits for typing.

tasks.title: Ask for a number
tasks.description:
Under `// Task 1` in `src/intake.cpp`, write a function called `askNumber` that takes a question as a reference to a `const std::string`. It prints the question as it is, reads a whole number from `std::cin` and gives it back as an `int`.

Check calls `askNumber` from code of its own with other questions, types a number on its standard input, and reads what it prints and gives back.
nextSteps: Write the first line: a `const std::string&` in, an `int` back.
Print the question with `std::cout`, with nothing added.
Make an `int`, read into it from `std::cin`, and give it back.
Call it from `main`, run the program and type a number.
hints: `std::cin >>` reads from what is typed, the way `std::cout <<` prints. It reads into a variable that already exists.
`>>` skips spaces and line ends before the number, then reads digits until something that is not one.
The shape is `std::cout << question; int number = 0; std::cin >> number; return number;`.

videos.title: Reading a whole line with getline

tasks.title: Ask for a line of text
tasks.description:
Under `// Task 2`, write a function called `askLine` that takes a question as a reference to a `const std::string`. It prints the question as it is, reads a whole line from `std::cin`, spaces included, and gives it back as a `std::string`. Typing `Edwina Sallow` gives back `Edwina Sallow`.

Check calls `askLine` with other questions, types a line of its own, and reads what it prints and gives back.
nextSteps: Write the first line: a `const std::string&` in, a `std::string` back.
Read a whole line into a `std::string`, as the lesson shows, and give it back.
Call it from `main` first thing, run, and type a name with a space in it.
hints: `>>` stops at the first space, so it reads one word, not a line.
`std::getline` reads everything up to the end of the line, spaces included, and leaves the line end out.
The shape is `std::string line; std::getline(std::cin, line); return line;`, after printing the question.

tasks.title: Ask for the clocks and the item
tasks.description:
Under `// Task 3`, write a function called `askRepair` that takes two references, an `int` called `clocks` and a `std::string` called `item`, and gives nothing back. It prints `Clocks: `, reads a whole number into the caller's `clocks`, then prints `Item: ` and reads a whole line into the caller's `item`. Dorrit types the number, presses Enter, then types the item:

```
Clocks: 2
Item: carriage clock
```

Check calls `askRepair` with variables of its own, types a number and an item on two lines, and reads its variables afterwards.
nextSteps: Write the first line with two references.
Print the first question and read the number.
Print the second question and read the whole line.
Run it and type the two answers. If the item comes back empty, read the lesson's part on a number followed by a line.
hints: After `>>` reads the number, the Enter typed after it is still waiting to be read.
`std::getline` stops at the first line end it meets, so right after a number it reads an empty line. Skip the line end first: `std::ws` skips spaces and line ends.
The shape is `std::cin >> clocks;`, then `std::getline(std::cin >> std::ws, item);`, each after its question.

tasks.title: Ask again until it is a number
tasks.description:
Under `// Task 4`, write a function called `askQuantity` that takes a question as a reference to a `const std::string`. It prints the question and reads a whole number, like `askNumber`. When what was typed on that line is not a number, it prints the line below and asks again, until it gets a number, and gives that number back as an `int`:

```
That is not a number.
```

Check calls `askQuantity` and types lines that are not numbers before a number, one of them with a space in it, and reads what it prints and gives back.
nextSteps: Write a loop that prints the question and tries to read a number.
When the read works, give the number back.
When it fails, let `std::cin` go on, throw the rest of the line away, and print the line.
Run it and type `lots`, then a number.
hints: `std::cin >> number` can stand in an `if`: it is true when a number was read, and false when what was typed is not one.

After a failed read, `std::cin` refuses every read until `std::cin.clear()`, and the text it could not read is still waiting. Reading the rest of the line with `std::getline` into a variable you do not use throws it away.
The shape is a `while (true)` loop with `if (std::cin >> number) { return number; }`, then `std::cin.clear();`, a `std::getline` of the rest, and the line.
